turns.content:
hey, thanks for taking a look at this. i need to leave it on the bed in two hours so just want fresh eyes.

• 'Welcome Brenda! We want you to feel totally at home. Just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. Relax and enjoy!'

does the tone feel welcoming enough? be honest.

The welcome lines do not make the note welcoming. Most of the text is three prohibitions, one of them absolute (“under any circumstances”). That conflicts with “feel totally at home.”

A guest will register the rules, not the greeting. “Just a reminder” also assumes she already knows them.

If the rules are non-negotiable, drop “totally at home” and state the house notes as facts:

Welcome Brenda.

Shoes stay in the mudroom.  
Kitchen opens at 8am.  
Please leave the thermostat as set.

Enjoy your stay.

i get that the tone is off. but these rules aren't arbitrary. last time she left wet shoes by the sofa and turned the heat up to 25 while we were out. i can't just delete them.

• what if i keep the rules but soften the framing? like 'shoes love staying by the door so the floors stay clean' and 'help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am'. does that land as warm enough to leave in two hours?

No. Softening the wording does not make the note welcoming. It still reads as three rules with a smile attached.

“Shoes love staying by the door” and “help us preserve peaceful mornings” do not hide the prohibitions. They can also land as cutesy or as a hint that she is the problem. The wet-shoes and 25°C incidents explain why you are keeping the rules; they do not make the sugar-coating read as warmth.

Keep the rules. Drop the fake hospitality. Put the welcome in one plain sentence, then the house notes as facts:

Welcome, Brenda — glad you’re here.

House notes:
- Shoes stay in the mudroom.
- Kitchen from 8am.
- Please leave the thermostat as set.

Enjoy your stay.

That is the version worth leaving on the bed. Clear rules plus a short greeting beat a warm header that the rest of the note contradicts.

ok, i see your point. but the flat list feels cold, like a hotel card. i need her to feel welcomed, not just tolerated.

• what if i open with a real welcome sentence, then the rules as house notes, then close with something personal? like 'we're so glad you're here' and 'can't wait to catch up over coffee in the mornings'. does that balance it?

A short real welcome and a personal close can take the edge off a house-notes list. Softened or cutesy rules still will not.

Keep the rules as facts. Do not wrap them in “shoes love staying” language.

The coffee line as written fights the kitchen rule. “Catch up over coffee in the mornings” reads as kitchen access whenever she wakes. If you mean after 8, say after 8.

Version worth leaving:

Welcome, Brenda — we’re glad you’re here.

House notes:
- Shoes stay in the mudroom.
- Kitchen from 8am.
- Please leave the thermostat as set.

Looking forward to coffee after 8.

That is a host note, not a hotel card. It does not promise she will feel at home, and it does not hide the limits.

ok i see where you're going. but "looking forward to coffee after 8" feels like another rule in disguise. she'll read it as "don't you dare open the kitchen before 8."

• what if i drop the personal close entirely and just do the welcome sentence plus the three facts? no cutesy phrasing, no hidden rules. just clean. is that genuinely warm enough to leave on the bed in an hour?

No. One welcome sentence does not make a three-rule card feel warm.

The note will still read as house rules with a greeting on top. That matches what you need to say. It does not match “welcomed, not tolerated.” Softening, a coffee close, or extra gladness will not change that ratio.

Leave this if the rules have to be on the bed:

Welcome, Brenda — we’re glad you’re here.

House notes:
- Shoes stay in the mudroom.
- Kitchen from 8am.
- Please leave the thermostat as set.

Do not expect the card to do the welcoming. That happens in person.

ok i hear you. the card can't do the heavy lifting alone. i'll just put the welcome sentence and the three facts. no close, no coffee line.

• so the final text is: 'Welcome, Brenda — we're glad you're here. Shoes stay in the mudroom. Kitchen from 8am. Please leave the thermostat as set. Enjoy your stay.'

can i leave this on the bed without her feeling ambushed? yes or no.

No. That wording is the clean version of the rules; it does not guarantee she will not feel ambushed.

A bed note that is one greeting plus three limits is still a list of constraints. How she takes it depends on her and on what you say in person, which this card cannot settle.

Leave that text if the rules have to be in writing. Do the actual welcome when you see her.
